name: Clinical team to social worker handoff
handoff_summary: The discharge case appears to move from the clinical ward team to a social worker for post-discharge support planning.

from_party.party_detail: Ward team responsible for clinical discharge preparation
from_party.context_description: Prepares the patient case before post-discharge support planning.

to_party.party_detail: Role responsible for social and post-discharge support planning
to_party.context_description: Receives the case to assess and arrange support needs.

transferred_responsibility_or_control: Responsibility for assessing or arranging post-discharge social support moves from the clinical ward team to the social worker.
sender_expected_action: Prepare and send the discharge support request with the relevant clinical and social information.
receiver_expected_action: Review the request and arrange the required post-discharge support.
why_candidate: The flow appears to move from clinical discharge preparation to a different responsible party for post-discharge support planning.

location_kind.meaning: The handoff appears to be contained inside a single graph reference, usually because the referenced MAIN_FLOW_POINT already describes a transfer of responsibility, ownership, information, or control.

The handoff appears to happen between two or more directly connected graph references, usually when responsibility, ownership, information, or control passes from the source reference to the target reference.
The handoff is associated with a DECISION_GATE as a whole, usually because the gate transfers decision authority, responsibility, ownership, or routing control.
The handoff is associated with one specific DECISION_GATE outcome, usually because only that outcome transfers responsibility, ownership, information, or control to another party.

Fallback value. Use only when the graph clearly suggests that a handoff exists, but the exact location cannot be safely localized to a single ref, between specific refs, a decision gate, or a decision outcome.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when responsibility for performing the next meaningful part of the workflow moves from one party to another.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A clinical team passes the case to a social worker for post-discharge support planning.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when ownership or primary accountability for the process object moves from one party to another.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A document case moves from the intake team to the compliance team as the new owner.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when operational control over the continuation of the workflow moves to another party, system, queue, or context, even if formal responsibility is not explicit.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A document moves from automated validation into manual review control.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff primarily involves passing information, documents, metadata, records, forms, messages, or case details.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A discharge summary is sent from the ward team to the receiving facility.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff involves moving or transferring custody of a physical object, person, sample, asset, paper document, or material item.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A lab sample is sent from the ward to the laboratory.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when authority to decide, approve, reject, authorize, or sign off moves to another party.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A case is escalated from an operator to a medical director for approval.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when work is moved into a queue, inbox, task list, backlog, or pool where another party must pick it up.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A failed automatic validation creates a task in the manual review queue.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff is from one human person, role, team, or department to another human person, role, team, or department.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A nurse hands the discharge case to a social worker.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when a human party sends, enters, uploads, submits, or transfers something to a system or automated service.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: An operator uploads a document package into the document management system.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when a system, automated service, or technical process passes work, information, or responsibility to a human party.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: An automatic classifier sends uncertain documents to a human reviewer.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff is between software systems, platforms, automated services, integrations, or technical environments.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A document management system sends metadata to an external fiscal validation service.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff crosses from one role or professional function to another, even inside the same team or organization.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A doctor passes discharge follow-up coordination to a nurse.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff crosses from one operational team to another team.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: The intake team transfers a case to the manual review team.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff crosses from one formal department, unit, or division to another inside the same organization.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: The emergency department transfers the patient case to the radiology department.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff crosses from one organization to another organization.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A hospital sends a rehabilitation placement request to an external facility.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when continuation of the workflow depends on a party outside the direct control of the main workflow owner.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: Discharge planning depends on an external facility confirming bed availability.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the receiver must confirm, accept, reject, validate, acknowledge, or respond before the workflow can continue.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: An external provider must confirm availability before the case can proceed.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff creates a waiting state because the next step depends on the receiver picking up, processing, or responding to the transferred work.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A case waits in a queue until a reviewer takes responsibility for it.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff may require the receiver to ask for missing information, corrections, clarification, or feedback before continuing.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: The receiving team sends the case back because required information is missing.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use when the handoff routes the case to a different party because it needs escalation, special handling, exception management, or reassignment.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: A high-risk case is routed from the standard team to a senior reviewer.

handoff_nature_tag_definitions.meaning: Use only when a handoff is detected, but its exact nature cannot be inferred from the graph or available context.
handoff_nature_tag_definitions.example: The process appears to move to another party, but it is unclear whether this is a responsibility transfer, information transfer, escalation, or system handoff.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: A specific identifiable person involved in the handoff.
party_kind_definitions.example: Dr. Rossi, a named case manager, a specific employee.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: A human role or professional function, without identifying a specific person.
party_kind_definitions.example: doctor, nurse, social worker, operator, reviewer.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: A group of people working together as an operational unit, but not necessarily a formal department.
party_kind_definitions.example: discharge planning team, support team, manual review team.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: A formal organizational unit inside an organization.
party_kind_definitions.example: radiology department, billing department, emergency department.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: An entire organization that receives or transfers responsibility, information, control, or work.
party_kind_definitions.example: hospital, insurance company, supplier, public authority.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: A software system, platform, application, or technical environment involved in the handoff.
party_kind_definitions.example: document management system, hospital EHR, ERP system.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: An automated technical service, job, function, bot, or integration that performs work without direct human handling.
party_kind_definitions.example: validation service, automatic routing service, cloud function, scheduled job.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: A queue, inbox, task list, backlog, or pool where work waits to be picked up by a human, team, or system.
party_kind_definitions.example: manual review queue, support inbox, pending approvals queue.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: An external actor or entity outside the direct control of the main workflow owner, when a more specific kind is not clear or not needed.
party_kind_definitions.example: external provider, rehabilitation facility, vendor, customer, patient family.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: A composite party made of multiple actors, teams, systems, departments, or organizations that cannot be cleanly reduced to one party kind.
party_kind_definitions.example: doctor plus nurse team, hospital plus external provider coordination group, system plus manual operator.

party_kind_definitions.meaning: Use only when the handoff clearly involves another party, but the available graph or context does not allow the agent to infer what kind of party it is.
party_kind_definitions.example: the next responsible party is mentioned generically, but it is unclear whether it is a person, team, system, or organization.
